title: Ghosts Beat Snakes, Sharks and Spiders Combined in AI Fear Prompts
summary: Magic Hour found 209 creators explicitly pairing ghosts or haunted scenes with fear language, 53% more than the 137 creators depicting snakes, sharks or spiders combined.
body_markdown:
## Quick answer


**Ghosts and haunted scenes appeared with fear language among 209 creators—53% more than snakes, sharks, and spiders combined (137 creators).**


This analysis covers completed Magic Hour visual-generation projects created from June 1 through September 18, 2026.


Ghosts are winning the nightmare economy. In a privacy-safe analysis of completed Magic Hour visual-generation projects, 209 creators explicitly paired ghosts or haunted scenes with fear language. Only 137 creators did the same with snakes, sharks or spiders combined.


Ghostly fear appeared for 53% more creators than the three real creatures together. Ghosts led the combined creature group in every month of the analysis window.


## Ghosts won every month


Ghosts led the deduplicated snakes, sharks or spiders group in each monthly slice: 23 creators versus 19 in June, 46 versus 24 in July, 72 versus 48 in August, and 71 versus 48 from September 1 through September 18.


The combined creature row counts each creator once even when that creator depicted more than one of the three creatures.


## What the finding means


The analysis measures what Magic Hour creators asked visual AI tools to depict. It does not measure what people fear in real life, diagnose any individual creator, or prove why ghosts appeared more often.


One possible interpretation is that a ghost is unusually flexible visual shorthand. It can be eerie, frightening, sad, comic or nostalgic, while a shark or spider tends to pull a scene toward a narrower kind of threat. That explanation is a hypothesis, not a measured result.


## Methodology


Magic Hour analyzed completed projects from Text to Video, Image to Video, Animation, AI Image, AI GIF and Storyboard created from June 1 through September 18, 2026. The unit of analysis was the distinct creator, not the number of projects.


The analysis retained the latest warehouse row for each project and excluded failed, deleted, disabled, templated, automated free-tool and blank-prompt records. Exact normalized prompts used by five or more creators in the same tool and month were removed to reduce copied text, shared inspirations and defaults.


A category qualified only when a subject term appeared within eight words of explicit fear language such as afraid, scared, terror, terrified, nightmare, panic, horror, phobia, danger, attack, escape or threat. Category-specific exclusions removed unrelated uses such as ghostwriting, ghost kitchens, Shark Tank, loan sharks, spider plants and Spider-Man.


Adult or sexual context, political and celebrity names, and prominent copyrighted-character terms were excluded before counting. Raw prompts were reviewed internally to refine the rules, but no prompt text is published.


## Privacy and limitations


No raw prompts, creator identities, project identifiers, uploaded media or generated outputs are published. Every headline comparison contains more than 100 distinct creators.


Magic Hour users are not representative of all AI creators or the public. Dictionary matching can miss translations, synonyms and indirect descriptions. Stored prompt text was not checked against the finished output. The results are descriptive and do not establish cause.


## Citation-ready finding


Among completed Magic Hour visual-generation projects created from June 1 through September 18, 2026, 209 creators explicitly paired ghosts or haunted scenes with fear language, compared with 137 creators for snakes, sharks or spiders combined. Ghostly fear appeared for 53% more creators and led in every month of the analysis window.


Source: Magic Hour aggregated, privacy-safe usage data. Aggregate tables, category definitions and reproducible SQL are available from Magic Hour Research.
